title: What the assigned empirical studies say about Chevron
shortTitle: What the assigned empirical studies say about Chevron
summary: The notes distinguish Supreme Court and circuit-court studies and caution against assuming that an announced deference framework determines outcomes uniformly.
notes:
Eskridge and Baer’s study examined 1,014 Supreme Court cases from the 1983 through 2005 Terms involving agency statutory interpretations. The quoted account reports express Chevron use in 8.3 percent and no identifiable deference regime in 53.6 percent. The authors describe a continuum of approaches rather than a uniform doctrinal revolution. A later analysis by Salmanowitz and Spamann proposed that the parties’ and amici’s presentation of Chevron helped explain whether the Court discussed it. These are reports of particular datasets and arguments, not current measurements. (Printed 964–965.)

The notes report that Barnett and Walker’s study of circuit opinions from 2003 through 2013 found fidelity to Chevron, and list other studies with differing results about whether review frameworks affected outcomes. The source also identifies work on Chevron’s gradual rise in lower courts. Supreme Court docket selection, whether a study counts all relevant cases or only those citing a doctrine, the time window, and the outcome being measured can change what an empirical claim means. (Printed 965.)

The casebook states that, at the time of its writing, it lacked empirical work measuring Loper Bright’s effect. That statement is part of the assigned historical source. The study takeaway is to preserve each claim’s court level, dates, denominator, and measure rather than convert the notes into an unsupported forecast.
